title: Expected Shortfall and Coherence

maps.tested: Consistently reported as one of the easier numericals: 'ES calculation: simple one', 'ES calculation easy'. The difficulty is not the arithmetic but knowing which observations enter the tail average.
maps.specifics: One recall captures the exact trap: 'ES numerical given the sample and resampling values: I took the average of all 5 samples, it could be average of 4 losses or 5.' That off-by-one on tail membership is the intended distractor. A second reported form is ES as the average of tail VaRs read off a confidence-level table, and a third is ES within filtered historical simulation. Also the coherence argument: ES is subadditive, VaR is not.

selectors.name: ES from a sample and its resamples
selectors.what: ES of a loss sample at confidence alpha, or the bootstrap estimate from resamples: with n losses the tail holds (1 - alpha) x n losses and ES is their average, so exactly which losses enter the average (4, 5 or 6) is what is tested. The best bootstrap ES is the mean of the resample ESs.
selectors.theory: The tail has (1 - alpha) x n observations; the VaR is the (1 - alpha) x n + 1 th highest loss, the highest loss outside the tail, and is left out of the average. Averaging one fewer loss gives a higher-confidence ES, one more drags the VaR observation in. Each resample gives its own VaR and ES, and the bootstrap point estimate is the average across resamples, not any single resample's figure.

selectors.name: ES as the average of tail VaRs
selectors.what: ES estimated by slicing the tail into n equal-probability slices, reading the n - 1 tail VaRs at confidence levels above alpha from a table and averaging them; compared with the 99% VaR that 97.5% ES replaces under FRTB.
selectors.theory: The VaR at alpha itself is excluded and the sum is divided by n - 1, not n. The estimate rises toward the true ES as the number of slices grows, so coarse slicing understates ES. For normal losses 97.5% ES (mu + 2.338 sigma) is close to 99% VaR (mu + 2.326 sigma); for a heavier tail the 97.5% ES is considerably greater.

selectors.name: ES within filtered historical simulation
selectors.what: How ES is obtained under filtered historical simulation: fit an asymmetric GARCH, standardise returns by the model volatility, bootstrap them and scale by the forecast volatility for tomorrow, then average the simulated losses beyond the VaR.
selectors.theory: FHS is a semi-parametric bootstrap that scales by the forecast of tomorrow's volatility, not the volatility of the day drawn; it can exceed the largest historical loss (basic HS cannot), keeps the correlation structure, and extends easily to ES, the partial answer to the worry that FHS VaR neglects extremes.

selectors.name: Coherence: ES subadditive, VaR not
selectors.what: Which risk measure satisfies the coherence conditions (monotonicity, positive homogeneity, translation invariance, subadditivity): ES is coherent and subadditive, VaR is subadditive only for elliptical distributions such as the normal and can fail for skewed or very heavy-tailed losses.

selectors.name: Standard errors of risk-measure estimators
selectors.what: How the standard error of a quantile, VaR or ES estimator behaves: it rises as the quantile moves further into the tail and falls with the sample size n; ES estimators can have much larger standard errors than VaR for heavy-tailed distributions.
